items.title: Norris wants F1 race ban for Colapinto
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Lando Norris says Franco Colapinto should face a Formula 1 race ban for his error during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix that took Norris, Colapinto and Pierre Gasly out of the race.

After a fairly processional first 30-plus laps of the Baku race, Colapinto had a massive lock-up while entering Turn 1 on a safety car restart while running in 10th place, seemingly caught out by the rate of deceleration from the Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli ahead of him.

He avoided hitting Antonelli but instead had to hug the inside wall and never scrubbed off anywhere near enough speed, ploughing into Alpine team-mate Gasly in the braking zone, with the chain reaction also eliminating Norris.

It was an error that Norris, who had had a particularly difficult weekend up to then and had his own Turn 1 mistake just before the safety car, did not take kindly to.

Norris stressed that he had not seen the replay at the time of speaking but said: "I think the FIA should be more strict and start handing out bans for this kind of stuff. It's just careless from people.

"It costs a lot of money, all my parts are in the bin now. People should just get banned, because that's not driving that deserves to be in Formula 1."

On whether race leader George Russell's approach to the restart bunched up the field too much, he said: "George can do what he wants.

"In Formula 1 I think you expect drivers to anticipate things, know grip is going to be low, know tyre temps are low - they weren't even that low.

"In Formula 1 you want to be against the best drivers in the world, and when stuff like this happens, it's because...yeah, [it] shouldn't be there."

He reiterated later that he wanted "at least a one-race ban" for this kind of crash.

A race ban in F1 requires a driver to amass 12 penalty points in a 12-month period - which has become a lot less likely since the FIA revised its approach to penalty points, seeking only to penalise what it perceived as actively dangerous driving or unsportsmanlike conduct.

By virtue of a number of yellow flag infringements, Colapinto is joint-top with Carlos Sainz in the current penalty points leaderboard - but, pending a verdict on this incident, that still means only four points, so there is no precedent under the current system by which he would be banned for the next round.

Colapinto, for his part, was immediately apologetic on the radio and maintained that tone in his media appearance.

"I was out of control completely. Not a lot more to say than sorry to the team, to Pierre, of course, to all the factory," he said.

"I'm sorry to Lando also. I'm sorry to everyone. It was a big mistake, of course."

He didn't respond specifically to Norris's suggestion of a race ban but said: "I do expect to get something [in terms of a penalty], of course. I don't know, I'm not a steward."

A 10-second penalty was assessed against Colapinto as the Baku race concluded - but as he did not reach the finish, this is now set to be converted to a grid drop.

items.title: Russell denies Verstappen in Azerbaijan GP punctuated by two safety cars
items.author: Jack Benyon
items.content:
George Russell ended a barren run without a Formula 1 victory in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix by just 0.196s over Max Verstappen, with championship leader Kimi Antonelli recovering to fifth from 16th in part thanks to a pair of safety cars for crashes.

Russell did everything a leader on a street circuit with a long straight on it should do: he got a good start, immediately cleared the one-second overtake window, and had extended his lead to 12 seconds by the time of the first pit stops.

His biggest early cause for concern was "nibbling" the wall at the exit of Turn 15 on lap 25 of 51, but he otherwise ran untroubled until Alex Albon crashing at Turn 4 on lap 31 erased his advantage.

The safety car benefitted Russell's team-mate Kimi Antonelli most.

Championship leader Antonelli started 16th and actually lost a spot at the start, then took 17 laps to pass seven cars and make it to the points-paying positions. While his progress wasn't as rapid as his comeback win at Monza from 19th, it was risk-averse and steadier with the championship lead likely in mind.

He caught and passed Franco Colapinto after erasing a just under four-second gap for ninth and then was gifted eighth when Lando Norris's disappointing race continued as the McLaren driver went straight on with a lock-up at Turn 1.

At the point of the safety car Antonelli was eighth and 35s off Russell, but the safety car bunched the field to give him a better chance of progressing and allowed him to switch to the favoured soft tyre.

He immediately made up a place on the restart as a massive melee broke out at Turn 1.

A massive, near-comical lock-up from Colapinto smashed him into Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly - who'd been seventh on the restart - and also took Norris out, while Liam Lawson was also spun in the concertina effect behind by Arvid Lindblad. "I love getting taken out by my team-mate," said a sarcastic Lawson, while Alpine lost a double-points finish in the chaos - much to Gasly's displeasure and Colapinto's apologies.

In the highest-pressure scenario of having Verstappen behind, Russell absolutely nailed the restart on lap 39 but Verstappen remained in overtake mode range until three laps later, and then Verstappen set the fastest lap of the race to close back in - refusing to accept defeat.

All the way until two laps to go Verstappen stayed within range and subjected Russell to pressure, until Russell finally built a 1.4s gap, but then Verstappen closed back in on the run to finish line on the final lap once both had cleared the scene of Valtteri Bottas's crashed Cadillac.

But Russell was just able to hold on for his first win since the Austria GP in late-June.

"After the double-yellow I had no boost, had no power," said Russell after the race.

Verstappen charged through the field from his eighth-place starting spot in the early stages, and despite some bickering between himself and his engineer over the mediums, and intense early pressure from Isack Hadjar, drove a fine race to take second. He'd passed Oscar Piastri for second already after the first safety car restart.

Hadjar bagged an amazing result to take third after three races out injured, and was clearly faster in the early stages and played a great team-mate race by offering to stay behind Verstappen.

Fourth-place finisher Charles Leclerc was passed by both the Red Bulls and appeared to struggle for pace, making a podium unlikely on the day, and it could have been worse had Piastri hadn't taken himself out of the battle with a lock-up at the first corner that sent him into the runoff area, compounding McLaren's disappointing day.

Antonelli received damage to his floor after being clipped by Ollie Bearman on the first safety car restart, and initially struggled to clear Lewis Hamilton, but finally got past five laps after the second restart at Turn 1 and went no further, taking fifth in another comeback drive.

Hamilton was the only driver in the top 10 other than Russell to finish where he started, perhaps reflecting Ferrari's race pace struggles.

Behind him, the Alpine-induced crash created chaos and brought a host of cars well out of points contention into play.

In-the-news Esteban Ocon may be losing his Haas seat but vaulted team-mate Bearman between the two safety cars, but then was bested on the last lap by just 0.030s - with Lindblad stealing the spot at the line. He avoided a penalty for the Lawson incident and made some opportunistic overtakes to make the best of a tough weekend with seventh place.

Ocon took eighth ahead of Bearman, while the upgraded Williams bagged a point through Carlos Sainz, who was as low as 19th after his early stop.

Hulkenberg missed out on the point with 11th, ahead of Lawson, Gabriel Bortoleto, Piastri and Sergio Perez.

items.title: The surprise ex-F1 driver aiding Alpine's revival
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Alpine has revealed a surprise asset supporting its Formula 1 revival this season - ex-Red Bull driver and podium finisher Daniil Kvyat.

Kvyat, who started 110 grands prix from 2014 to 2020, quietly rejoined the Enstone team this year as a simulator driver.

He had a stint at Alpine in 2021 as its reserve driver, having spent his F1 career racing for Red Bull's teams across multiple stints split by a year on the sidelines in 2018, when he was a simulator driver for Ferrari.

Kvyat's role has been kept under wraps as he shares simulator duties with Alpine reserve drivers Paul Aron and Kush Maini.

This includes development work but also race weekend support duties when Aron is required to be on-site at flyaway races.

During race weekends, Kvyat keeps in contact with Alpine race driver Pierre Gasly, who he was team-mate to at Red Bull's junior team and has a good relationship with, to share direct feedback.

Kvyat is understood to have played a significant role in Alpine's in-weekend turnarounds in Japan and Canada.

Alpine is enjoying a much improved season in F1 as the new rules and its switch to Mercedes engines have launched it back to the head of the midfield.

Kvyat has raced and/or tested NASCAR, top-level sportscar and Formula E machinery since his F1 exit, and had a role as a reference driver racing against an autonomous vehicle in Abu Dhabi.

He is competing in Japan's Super GT series this year in the GT300 category, alongside veteran driver Takashi Kogure. The pair are 16th in the points with a best class finish of sixth.

items.title: Gary Anderson: Breaking down Audi's colossal F1 upgrade
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
Audi should get the prize for the most comprehensive car update this season given how many new parts it has brought to Azerbaijan.

However, it’s all about how it works together - and not just about a jumble of parts.

Starting as always with the front wing, it looks like a completely new package. The mainplane now has a more defined upsweep going outboard, still integrated into the footplate of the front wing endplate, while the flap assembly appears to be loaded further inboard.

Both of these changes will improve the consistency of the airflow going around the inside of the front tyre, especially when varying degrees of steering lock are applied.

The increase in the three-dimensional effect on the leading edge of the front wing endplate will increase the outwash, as will the reduction in the camber of the blue-highlighted horizontal vane coming out of that endplate and the increase in size and detail of the small orange vane just in front of the tyre.

Audi is more or less alone in that its front wing actuator is mounted on the wing’s upper surface. As opposed to hiding it, Audi has decreased its size.

All of these developments could be grouped together as one development to better manage the airflow going around the inside and outside of the front tyre and wheel assembly.

F1 being an open-wheel formula, the tyres are one of the most obtrusive blockages that F1 teams have to aerodynamically deal with. Changes in this area can have consequences further downstream, so these changes have led Audi into a very comprehensive update package.

Audi's unique (until McLaren introduced its new sidepod package) sidepod leading edge and radiator inlet have also been modified in that there is now a slightly more bulbous section at the floor leading edge. This is probably to be more sympathetic to the airflow as it separates to go under the floor’s leading edge and/or around the side of the floor.

The actual sidepods have also changed, with the upper surface now allowing more downwash and, with that, a change to the cooling exit system.

Audi has gone from an array of louvres to a more common opening. This has required the magenta-highlighted section to be made into two sections: the front part with an opening at the rear and the rear section’s leading edge blocked off, which looks very bulbous.

Continuing that theme of managing the airflow around the front tyres, the next question is - how can you optimise that new and revised flow structure?

This magenta-highlighted outer floor edge doesn’t look very different. There seems to be a small more aggressive turned-up section just behind the bargeboard area; it’s simply a knife edge which should, because of the difference in pressure on the top and bottom surfaces, produce a vortex along its length, helping to seal that area of the floor.

To complete this floor detail, Audi has also revisited the vanes in front of the rear tyre contact patch. This is in line with what I said earlier about managing the airflow around the blockage created by the tyres.

Maximising the outwash in this area means there is less inwash, which disrupts the airflow structure to the diffuser, reducing its efficiency.

Small details also count, as they all add up. This area of the intersection between the halo and the leading edge of the headrest can very easily create turbulence that affects the stability of the driver’s head. This small vane will help to consistently manage some of that turbulence.

There are now four fairly large cooling exit openings. The cooling system works because of the pressure drop across the radiator cores: positive pressure on the inlet, negative pressure on the outlet. It’s very difficult to increase the positive pressure as that is generated by car speed, but a larger, better-positioned opening can fairly easily increase the negative pressure at the exit. The important thing is to minimise the downforce losses that any of these openings induce.

Audi has also changed the angle of support that the diffuser sides are getting from these longer and repositioned floor stays that are highlighted in green.

Nothing has been left unaddressed. The rear wing trailing edge trim details have also come under review.

The aero, as with the cooling exits, is in reality circuit-dependent, so depending on the circuit requirements it can be altered as the race weekend progresses.

The battle in that midfield is just as intense, if not more so, than the battle up front. Every single point has potential $ signs in front of it.

Alpine introduced its big upgrade a few races ago, Williams came to Baku with a big upgrade, mainly a weight reduction - and now it’s Audi’s turn to air its developments. Who has taken the biggest step?

Hopefully we will get an indication this weekend. Audi has not fared well so far - but Baku is a strange circuit.

items.title: What explains Mercedes' most dominant performance of 2026
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
George Russell's pole-winning margin at Formula 1's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, 0.837 seconds, marked the biggest defeat for Mercedes' rivals in a 2026 qualifying session.

Even with just one car in Q3, Mercedes managed to beat its previous benchmark, of 0.785s, from the season-opening Australian GP weekend.

It undeniably has the best car and power unit package in Baku, but its rivals compromised themselves, making that gap bigger than it needed to be, as we explain.

Verstappen was down on power

Max Verstappen's Red Bull topped final practice and was looking like Mercedes’ closest challenger ahead of - and during - qualifying.

But that challenge failed to materialise, with Verstappen ending up eighth and a second and a half away from pole - his biggest time gap to pole of the season when he has set a lap in Q3.

His returning team-mate Isack Hadjar ended up as the lead Red Bull, in fourth, over half a second clear of Verstappen, who believed the majority of the gap could be explained by a mysterious power issue.

"The whole qualifying we were down on power, it was consistently half a second down to Isack's car," Verstappen said after qualifying.

"For whatever reason, we don't know why that happened in qualifying. Then in Q3, the middle lap coming out of the last corner, my battery didn't go to 100%, so I had to abort that lap.

"And too cold tyres then, because you don't have the speed, you don't have the power that you should have. Then when I tried on my final lap, with no power, the tyres [being] too cold and a yellow flag, it's not happening."

Verstappen encountered the yellow flags for Lando Norris's off in Q3, which also compromised him, so that 1.5s gap was far from representative.

If Verstappen had been able to put his three best sectors together, that deficit would have been 1.014s. That gap would have been reduced further with a clean final Q3 lap, with Lewis Hamilton believing Red Bull has the second-fastest car in Baku.

"It's a shame...the whole weekend we're doing a good job, I'm happy with the car and then it all just falls apart in qualifying because of problems out of my control," Verstappen said.

"It's a little bit this season...it's a bit too fragile at times."

The Red Bull drivers have suffered from an aerodynamic degradation issue all season but Verstappen said this wasn't present in Baku.

Asked by The Race if he might sacrifice his eighth place on the grid to take a new power unit, Verstappen said: "First just need to figure out what it is [the problem].

"Otherwise, if you have to run with that also tomorrow [in the race], it's not going to be a lot of fun. Let's see."

Verstappen did rank 20th out of 22 drivers in the speed trap (306.3km/h) across the start/finish line in qualifying, 11km/h down on Hadjar and over 18km/h down on Hamilton, the fastest driver through there.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies confirmed Verstappen's comments, saying his car developed an issue during qualifying that "got worse as the session went on".

"Not only did it bring a large straight-line speed deficit, but it also made our life very complicated with energy deployment and tyre preparation," said Mekies, who felt Verstappen's eighth place was "sort of a damage limitation" in the circumstances and added that Red Bull would "change the faulty parts" overnight.

McLaren's major straightline deficit

Verstappen wasn't the only driver complaining about straightline speed after qualifying.

Reigning world champion Lando Norris seems resigned to a difficult Azerbaijan GP considering McLaren's overall lack of aerodynamic efficiency and what he perceives to be a particular straightline deficit on his car compared to the sister McLaren of Oscar Piastri.

"The guys say everything's working as expected, but when you see eight tenths to the top, it's painful," said Norris. "Our time losses are in the straights. That's another area we just need to look at, because we're just a step worse to Mercedes in everything straightline-related.

"I've been comfortable in the car the whole weekend. My last lap I made a mistake and I paid the price, but I'm at a point in the championship where I kind of have to go for pole, or I kind of die trying. Of course, I paid the price for pushing too much, but it is what it is.

“It's been tough, especially with my car. We have to understand why I'm basically having to push more than Oscar to try and make up for my straightline speed [deficit].”

Team principal Andrea Stella said McLaren was investigating Norris's deficit and added: "It seems to be linked to the behaviour of the fuel injection, something that hopefully we will be able to or the adaptive systems should be able to improve [for the race].

"It looks occasionally [like] the power unit generates a bit less power. But this is a specific phenomenon; it's nothing to do with the overall behaviour of the power unit."

McLaren has brought a significant suite of upgrades to Baku, in an attempt to improve the car's efficiency - including a return for its revolving rear 'H-wing' that debuted at Monza - but Norris clearly felt further steps are needed to put McLaren in range of Mercedes.

"They have a very efficient car - they always have done for years," he added. "We need to take a big step in that direction if we want to be competitive in any straightline speed track for the rest of the season.

"But they also have just a good car in all the corners as well. They're just doing a better job in all areas, power unit and car."

Stella agreed. "While we have the same power unit, there's a few differences and I think it's fair to say that their package, chassis, ratios, power unit itself, it just seems to be more effective when it comes to generating top speed."

Hamilton rues Ferrari run plan and 'stupid tyres'

Hamilton's furious weaving before each of his push laps in Q3 highlighted that getting temperature into his front tyres was a factor in his challenge for a better grid slot falling away.

"I was weaving to try and save my life, and I still couldn't get these stupid tyres working," he said afterwards after he ended up sixth. "Such a pain in the ass. We've got to bring back some good tyres."

But tyre temperatures did not explain the full deficit to pole position as he ended up 1.3s adrift of Russell and nearly half a second behind Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.

Instead, the biggest time loss came from Hamilton having found himself running at the front of a train of cars so he was left without a slipstream.

Ferrari opted to change its run plan for Q3, doing push, cool, push laps rather than having a run and then changing tyres.

But its strategy backfired when cars Hamilton was running behind in the train - such as the two McLarens and Carlos Sainz's Williams - all were stopping, so got out of the way.

By the time things had shaken out, Hamilton had realised he was alone on track, more than 25 seconds behind Russell and simply towing his team-mate Charles Leclerc around.

At one point, realising what was happening, Hamilton asked his team for advice on what to do - but then told them not to worry as he would "look on the TV".

Based on what Hamilton had learned when he got a good tow in FP3 as he ended up third, the lack of a slipstream was very costly.

"It was six tenths," he said, when The Race asked how much the gain from getting the tow right was worth. "I didn't have one in that session."

Leclerc did, though, having followed Hamilton around, and that helped him secure his spot on the front row, albeit still well adrift of Russell.

Russell’s first pole position since the Austrian GP in late-June stands as his most compelling qualifying performance since his outstanding Friday and Saturday at the Barcelona GP.

He pointed to a slipstream that he felt gave him a tenth or two extra on a qualifying lap that "all perfectly came together" in Baku.

"I've been feeling in a great spot this whole weekend," said Russell. "I felt confident, I felt hooked up. I'm getting more and more on top of this car and what it requires, and it's just all feeling more intuitive."

Not that he believed this has come from nowhere. Asked whether he felt this represented a breakthrough, he suggested that wasn't the case and instead pointed to his improved form since the summer break.

"It's definitely just been perfectly hooked up for me this weekend so far," he said. "Me and my team have put so much work in to help me get on top of the limitations.

"Since the summer break it's been great and the performance has been substantially better than the results have shown."

Inevitably, Antonelli's absence from the track after clipping the inside wall at Turn 1 in Q1 means Russell didn't have the opportunity to prove he would have maintained his form from the build-up to qualifying and outpace his team-mate.

But Antonelli, who completed fewer practice laps than anyone after a hydraulic problem struck in FP1, with the resulting power unit change delaying his start to FP2, always seemed on the back foot.

"I did miss a lot of laps but in FP3 I felt pretty good," said Antonelli. "It was just a misjudgement, with the grip changing so much. An unnecessary one in Q1, and it’s a very good reminder that, like this, things don't go my way, so I need to do a much better job."

items.title: Sainz penalised for second yellow flag breach in one day
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Williams Formula 1 driver Carlos Sainz has received a five-place grid penalty for ignoring yellow flags during Azerbaijan Grand Prix qualifying.

The penalty denies Williams what was set to be its best grid position of the year, superseding Alex Albon's 11th place on the Monaco GP grid.

Remarkably, the sanction came on a day on which Sainz was already investigated - and found guilty - of a different yellow-flag breach, although on that occasion he was let off with a reprimand due to mitigating circumstances.

Sainz and Williams were originally hauled in front of the stewards after Friday morning practice for a yellow flag breach through Turn 4. The stewards ruled that Sainz "failed to sufficiently reduce speed" under the yellow flag - but felt there was sufficient mitigation to avoid the imposition of the grid penalty in "the very short period between the single yellow being displayed and Sainz entering the relevant marshalling sector".

No such mitigation was present in a different incident, recorded during the third qualifying segment. In fact, the stewards pointed out that Sainz received advanced warning from the team that a yellow flag was out on the approach to Turn 3, and simply failed to heed it sufficiently.

The warning in question was "yellow ahead, yellow ahead, [Lando] Norris, just do a lift, do a lift, and complete the lap" and then an apparent "clear-clear" that followed seconds later - seemingly creating a situation that led Sainz to believe the yellow flag was no longer acutely relevant.

"[Sainz] explained that he intended to demonstrate a reduction in speed across the yellow area as a whole," the stewards wrote as part of a lengthy explanation.

"He stated that he did not consider it necessary to reduce speed on the straight and instead intended to demonstrate his response when approaching and exiting Turn 3. He considered this to be a 'global lift' covering the consecutive yellow sectors. He further explained that the car [Norris] which had originally caused the yellow was no longer in the runoff area and that he expected the yellow flags to be withdrawn.

"The stewards did not accept this interpretation. Where consecutive marshalling sectors are subject to yellow-flag conditions, a driver must demonstrate a significant reaction to reduce speed in each individual yellow marshalling sector. A reduction in a subsequent sector cannot retrospectively satisfy the requirement applicable to the preceding yellow sector. The obligation is also not dependent on the driver's own assessment of whether the original hazard remains present within a particular part of the yellow sector."

McLaren driver Lando Norris had indeed vacated the relevant runoff by that point - but as the FIA stewards do not want the drivers to self-assess the validity of a yellow flag, they found the lack of any "meaningful reduction in speed" in the relevant marshalling sector was sufficient grounds for the penalty.

In addition to the five-position penalty, which demotes Sainz from ninth to 14th, he has also received two penalty points - taking him to a total of four for the 12-month period.

Sainz was not alone in incurring a grid penalty after Baku qualifying.

A three-position penalty has been assessed against Cadillac driver Sergio Perez for impeding McLaren driver Oscar Piastri in the opening segment.

The stewards wrote that Perez "received two radio warnings" from the team but still forced a needless lift from the McLaren driver through the Turns 18-19-20 section, by "not managing his preparation lap in accordance with specific traffic-management instructions" - namely the race director's order that a driver on a prep lap stay to the right-hand side and avoid weaving in front of incoming cars.

Because of the engine component penalties to the Aston Martin cars, however, Perez is only set to lose one position on the grid - going from 19th to 20th (the position he originally qualified in), behind team-mate Valtteri Bottas.

items.title: Winners and losers from F1 Azerbaijan GP qualifying
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
As a headline statistic, the biggest pole position margin yet around the streets of Baku points to an Azerbaijan Grand Prix qualifying session that might've lacked a bit of edge.

The reality was very different - and not just because of the contrasting fortunes of the two Mercedes drivers.

Here's our pick of winners and losers from Friday:

Loser: Kimi Antonelli (16th)

Given Mercedes' form so far this weekend, even with how compromised Antonelli's Thursday had proven this was still an easy (relatively speaking) 18 points just begging to be collected.

That's still a plausible outcome, but it sure will be harder now after an "unnecessary" impact with the inside barrier at Turn 1 during the opening segment.

"I had a lot more headwind compared to the lap before, so the front just was much stronger, and I turned in roughly in the same spot, but obviously the car turned more and I clipped the wall," Antonelli explained.

With 81 points in the pocket he can afford it - but there's no need to 'spend' a chunk of that margin this weekend. And maybe he won't - but he's put himself in a bit of a danger zone, in terms of grid position and the overtaking he will now need to do.

Winner: George Russell (1st)

Even before runaway championship leader Antonelli clipped the Turn 1 wall, Russell had been in formidable form. Without his team-mate for competition, that turned into pole position by a crushing margin of 0.837s.

Russell described himself as feeling "hooked up" from the start of the weekend, and while Max Verstappen, who he described as "the biggest threat", was hindered by yellow flags and a worsening engine issue, Russell always looked on target for pole position.

While it will take far more than one pole position, or even a victory on Saturday, to reignite his faded title chances, it's an important step in what Russell calls the "upward cycle" of improving his performances.

Loser: Max Verstappen (8th)

Max Verstappen reckoned he was losing half a second to Isack Hadjar because of an engine/power-related problem - and what was Verstappen's deficit to Hadjar in Q3? 0.581s.

OK, you'd expect Verstappen (who topped FP3) to beat Hadjar with the half-second deficit removed, especially after Hadjar's three-race injury lay-off, and he might still have done had he not caught a yellow flag on his final run.

On his second run prior to that, his battery didn't go to 100% for the run to the finish line, so that was another chance lost. Combined with the car's front-bottoming, which caused brake struggles, that meant a day that looked so promising turned into a nightmare for Verstappen.

Winner: Isack Hadjar (4th)

Ever a glass-half-empty driver in his time in F1 so far, Hadjar emphasised that with continuity instead of injury he would've "definitely" been on the front row here - instead missing out by 0.141s.

"Nothing outstanding," he added. But while a 2027 deal is already in his pocket it's certainly not a bad time to remind everyone, after three rounds of impressively workmanlike stand-in pace from Liam Lawson, that Hadjar has had serious speed this year.

And he did admit he has been happy about how he's eased himself into this weekend, at a track that is just waiting to catch you out.

"I told myself it's mandatory not to touch the wall or anything. For a comeback, there's no point taking a lot of risks. So I was really driving a bit under the limit the whole weekend in that very tight section - I think I just did that natural step in Q3."

Loser: Audi (17th and 18th)

The two heavily-upgraded Audis had not impressed very much in practice - but even so, the double Q1 exit looks like an aberration.

It's not just the power unit, Gabriel Bortoleto insisted.

"There were tracks like Monza where we were almost in Q3 and there are more straights than here. So I think it's something bigger that we need to understand," he said.

"I think it was better [earlier in the weekend], but still we were always on the edge of going out in Q1.

"The whole weekend we had no grip. If you don't have grip, you cannot go fast in the corners. If you don't go fast, you don't make a laptime. It's simple as that, and it's what other teams, when they go out in Q1, they probably say."

Team-mate Nico Hulkenberg was more cheery, in relative terms, arguing his Q1 exit was "mostly because of circumstances", specifically a yellow flag and a lost tow. And neither he nor Bortoleto is suggesting the upgrade is misfiring - but certainly it's proving no game changer for Baku.

Winner (then loser): Carlos Sainz (9th)

Sainz put Williams into Q3 for the first time this year as its significant car upgrade excelled on debut - although Sainz felt the result was an overachievement.

Alex Albon joined Sainz in Q2 as Williams escaped Q1 with both cars for the first time since July's British GP, which serves as evidence the FW48 is a more competitive beast in Baku.

But Sainz (who does still face a yellow flag investigation) felt his ninth place was a result of Williams nailing its tyre usage and run plan, and "some serious laps on the limit" from himself, to end up a little higher than it would be on pace alone.

He described the car as no different "in feel, just quicker" because it's lighter and has a bit more downforce - but the work done to achieve that has been immediately rewarded.

Sainz admitted that getting a noticeable result felt pretty good for him, too, after a year spent toiling further down the midfield - and described the laps to achieve that as "the highest stress of the season" because of the challenge threading through the twists of sector two on a gusty day and low-grip track.

What a shame, then, that a good deal of that good work was undone by a five-place grid drop for failing to slow for yellow flags.

Loser: Esteban Ocon (14th)

That aforementioned Hadjar lock-up in Q2 (on the right front, sending him into the Turn 15 escape road) had no real impact on his own qualifying - but did compound the misery of another French driver.

Ocon had three tenths in hand over team-mate Ollie Bearman coming into their final run in Q2, but couldn't match Bearman with his first effort after returning to the track - compromised by what he described as a "gust of wind", which seemingly sent him onto the outside kerb at Turn 16.

"And then I did the same laptime, again, [before] arriving to Turn 15. I don't know who went off [Hadjar], but I had to back off on the exit to make sure that I was not going to get any penalty," he vented.

"I did exactly the same laptime. So yeah, I lost, what, three-four tenths? Unbelievable. You know, I just have no words. It's different race weekend, same s**t. It's always something going on, on my side, if it's either the car, if it's something else, now yellow flag, safety cars, whatever.

"But I don't deserve all the s**t that I have on my back at the moment. So I don't know, I might need to take a good shower."

Winner: Alpine (7th & 10th)

Alpine took full advantage of Antonelli's absence to get both cars into Q3 - a good day for any midfield team when the top teams usually hog eight of the 10 spots at the top of the order.

Pierre Gasly managed to beat Max Verstappen - caveated by Verstappen's power issue, but still impressive - with his take being "great balance, great car, managed to get to Q3 pretty comfortably".

Franco Colapinto had more of a struggle, and his off into the Turn 15 run-off, blamed on a flatspot, also cost Gasly on his final flying lap. Gasly reckoned sixth-place qualifier Lewis Hamilton was also there for the taking without that.

A scruffy Q3, but it didn't matter, and Gasly's confident of keeping the rest of the 'midfield' behind.

Loser: Sergio Perez (20th)

The opportunity was there but, in the words of Perez, Cadillac "needed everything to go our way" to bag its first Q2 appearance.

Everything did not go its way.

Perez said Cadillac had the "wrong programme" in terms of how he and team-mate Valtteri Bottas prepared their laps. That went further awry when Bottas, who was due to provide the tow, was called to the weighbridge.

Then Perez had his final lap wrecked by Fernando Alonso going up the escape road at the Turn 15 left-hander ahead of him (a chain of events that meant the Aston Martin outqualified the Cadillac). To add insult to injury, Perez has also been assessed a three-place grid penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri.

The biggest shame is that we didn't get to see what Baku specialist Perez was capable of dragging out of the Cadillac. Because the form was there: 13th in FP2, 16th in FP3 - at the end of an eight-lap stint on the soft tyre on the latter occasion, too.

The positive for Perez and Cadillac is that this wasn't competitive reality setting in.

But not for the first time this season, they've probably been left frustrated by imperfections in their own execution. (To such an extent that a three-place grid drop for impeding Oscar Piastri doesn't make a great deal of difference.)

Winner: Oscar Piastri (3rd)

Although a front-row position was possible, as he was just one thousandth slower than Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, it was important for Piastri to get on top of McLaren team-mate Lando Norris after struggling in recent times.

Piastri described it as "not an easy weekend" for McLaren, so felt third on the grid was "a really good result".

Though he admitted that there have been some difficult laps amongst the good ones in Baku, overall he was encouraged with his own performance.

"On a personal level, I feel we've been building up well," said Piastri. "I was pretty happy with my laps in Q3."

Loser: Arvid Lindblad (15th)

Racing Bulls's hopes of significant mid-weekend gains have not so far come to fruition - the car looked outmatched in qualifying relative to some of its usual opposition, and is at risk of a particularly bad points day on Saturday if the two Alpines ahead benefit from some classic Baku chaos.

But while Lawson simply lamented the deficit on the straights, saying that Racing Bulls drivers are "trying to make up time that is not really there", for team-mate Lindblad such a quiet Q2 exit felt particularly sour.

"I'm a bit frustrated, more at myself than anything just because I feel that I didn't do something special like I normally do at the end of these qualifyings to put us in the final part," he regretted, admitting that his Thursday crash has compounded a shortage of confidence on braking.

"It's not been a good day, it's not been a good week. I just need to understand why I haven't been on it."

items.title: Why an F1 2026 standout regrets 'trying to be too special'
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Formula 1 rookie Arvid Lindblad delivered a scathing self-assessment of his performance so far at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix and will adjust his approach after “trying to be too special”.

The Baku weekend is proving arguably the toughest of Lindblad’s impressive first season in F1 as he crashed heavily in FP2 then made several mistakes in qualifying, which he ended slowest of the Q2 runners - his second-worst result of the year.

Lindblad said the Racing Bulls car has been “bad on the brakes” all through practice and qualifying and “just not been fun to drive” but said he shouldered responsibility for misjudging how aggressive to be in practice and shattering his own confidence.

His FP2 shunt, which was a result of taking too much speed into the narrow castle section and slamming heavily into the wall on the outside, came after crashing in second practice at the last race in Madrid too.

It has left Lindblad running a slightly older specification of parts compared to team-mate Liam Lawson, too, after Racing Bulls debuted a new front wing here.“I have no confidence, to be honest,” he said.

“Crashing yesterday, it doesn't help. I'm running a different car to Liam - as you'd expect when you crash, so that doesn't help.

“I've missed mileage as well, I missed the start of FP1, start of FP2 and then I crashed, I missed basically all the rest of it.

“I need to...I think there's stuff for me to learn on how to approach these weekends and manage them in a little bit of a better way because it's been two street circuits now where I've crashed in FP2 and hurt my trajectory to qualifying.

“We were struggling this weekend so probably Q3 wasn't possible but I definitely think if I'd managed things a little bit better we could have been in a better place going into this session and maybe, with a little bit of magic on my side, could have been in Q3.”

Lindblad said that not pulling something out of the bag was “what annoys me” most. He has started inside the top 10 for nine of the 14 grands prix – including the last seven in a row.

“I'm just mad at myself because, more than anything, in trying to be too special I've hurt my trajectory for when it matters and I haven't delivered in the moment,” he said.

“I enjoy being able to sort of switch off the brain and just send it when it matters and just go and have a bit of fun with it but this week I haven't really been able to do that and I think I could have just managed things in a better way to do that.”

Lawson was only 12th fastest on a weaker weekend for Racing Bulls than the fifth-placed team in the championship has come to expect this year.

He put that down to lacking engine performance compared to other teams in the midfield - and said that is partly where being on a knife-edge on the brakes has come from.

“We're just trying to make up time that is not really there and it's really tough,” said Lawson.

“Overall, if I look at my last lap of quali, it was the best lap I've done and with the right tow it would have been enough to get through to Q3, but that's pretty much everything going perfectly to plan and on a track like this that's obviously not happening for everybody.

“We've definitely struggled all weekend, it's been tough, but I think it's similar to Monza. These tracks with these really long straights we suffer a little bit more now than we did before.”

items.title: Antonelli crashes in Baku qualifying as Russell takes crushing pole
items.author: Jack Benyon
items.content:
George Russell took Azerbaijan Grand Prix pole by eight tenths with a sensational lap, a massive boost given his Mercedes Formula 1 team-mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli crashed and is due to start 16th in Baku.

The big drama unfolded with seven minutes left in Q1 as Antonelli whacked the inside wall at Turn 1 which immediately pointed the front left wheel in the wrong direction and punctured his tyre.

Multiple exchanges followed as Antonelli wanted to continue and try to bring the car back to the Mercedes garage, but his engineer Peter Bonnington told Antonelli to stop the car as there would be no chance to repair it even if he made it back.

Antonelli eventually pulled over and had to watch the remainder of Q1 through a fence.

He had been sixth when the accident happened but fell all the way to 15th with late improvements, which was at least enough to secure passage to Q2 - meaning he is due to start 16th, pending any grid penalties.

Left to fend for himself as the only Mercedes in the pole fight, Russell set benchmarks on his second Q3 run relatively early in the session, starting the final runs with a 0.435s advantage over Charles Leclerc.

He extended that to 0.946s before Leclerc completed his final run, but the Ferrari drive could only reduce the gap to 0.837s. Only three cars were within a second of Russell on the day.

Oscar Piastri beat McLaren team-mate Lando Norris on the second-to-last run and then Norris had a massive lock-up at Turn 3 on his final pole shot to wipe him out of contention, allowing Piastri to take third - just one thousandth behind Leclerc in the end - ahead of one of the stars of the session, Isack Hadjar.

In his first qualifying session since injuring his wrist and missing the first three races after the summer break, Hadjar repeatedly traded fast times with team-mate Max Verstappen through qualifying and only missed out on third thanks to Piastri's late improvement.

Norris took fifth, his previous lap good enough to beat a struggling Lewis Hamilton, who complained of tyre-warm-up woes throughout qualifying in the second Ferrari.

Alpine driver Pierre Gasly beat Verstappen to seventh - it looked like FP3 pacesetter Verstappen had to bail on his final flying lap for a yellow flag and reported after the session he had been down on power.

The upgraded Williams of Carlos Sainz delivered the stunning feat of reaching Q3 for the first time this year, in what must be a massive boost back at Williams's Grove factory after such a rough first part of the year. Sainz's contribution can't be underestimated given Alex Albon was 13th in Q2.

Franco Colapinto rounded out the top 10 after a lock-up at Turn 15 hampered his chances.

Haas's missed opportunity

Haas and Racing Bulls both lost their pair of cars in Q2, with the Alpines and Sainz making it through instead.

Ollie Bearman was knocked out at the very-last moment by Colapinto and had to settle for 11th, awaiting his first appearance in Q3 since the second round of the season in China in March.

His team-mate Esteban Ocon appeared to fare even worse as he'd regularly led Bearman and even run in the top 10 this weekend and in qualifying, but he had a lap deleted for track limits after going off at Turn 2 with his last flying run.

Liam Lawson and Albon split Bearman and Ocon, Albon a costly 0.372s adrift of team-mate Sainz, with Arvid Lindblad suffering a lap deletion for track limits at Turn 1, in 15th, ahead of Antonelli.

Audi's upgraded car exits in Q1

On a weekend where it has brought a significant upgrade package to Baku, Audi had two cars out in Q1 for the first time this year - a nightmare for a team that has regularly challenged to lead the midfield this season.

Hulkenberg had a small chance to escape Q1 before Fernando Alonso visiting the Turn 15 runoff caused a yellow flag that hampered Hulkenberg's chances.

Alonso followed the two Audis, with Sergio Perez splitting the Aston Martins. Some may have expected the Ferrari-powered Cadillac to have an advantage over the Aston Martin-Honda, but Cadillac's apparent plan to give Perez a tow failed when Bottas had to go to the weighbridge, and Perez also had to abandon his final lap due to Alonso's off.

Bottas had his final laptime deleted as he set it under double-waved yellows, and completed the order in 22nd.

items.title: MotoGP finally reveals 2027 calendar with Argentina + Adelaide dates
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
MotoGP has finally announced its long-awaited 2027 calendar, with no major surprises coming from the 22-race schedule for the first year of its new 850cc era.

There is nevertheless some minor movement for some of the season's races, the addition of a new race in Argentina, and the Australian Grand Prix's move from Phillip Island to Adelaide.

The season will kick off, as previously announced, in Thailand on March 7, one week later than in 2026, and is currently scheduled to then head directly to Qatar a week later - although The Race's sources in the paddock believes that could be alternated with October's Indonesian GP should the geopolitical situation in the Middle East remain complicated.

The series will then move to Brazil on April 4, the first part of a double-header that will then take MotoGP back to Argentina for the inaugural race at Buenos Aires' Autodromo Oscar y Juan Galvez, before rounding out the American trip two weeks later at the Circuit of the Americas in Texas.

Jerez will, as usual, host the first European race on May 9, a week before the slightly later French Grand Prix at Le Mans. That will be followed by races at Mugello, Barcelona, Assen, Sachsenring and Brno before the summer break.

Action will resume at Silverstone in August, one week later than usual, before Austria returns to an August date. Misano, Aragon, and a rescheduled Portuguese Grand Prix at Portimao come next before the overseas leg.

Japan starts the flyaway action on October 17 ahead of Malaysia, Indonesia, and the new Adelaide parklands race in mid-November, before the championship heads back to Europe for the traditional conclusion at Valencia on November 28.

items.title: What happened in F1 2026 Azerbaijan GP final practice
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
Red Bull Formula 1 driver Max Verstappen headed Mercedes' George Russell by a tenth of a second in a busy final practice session for the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Thursday pacesetter Russell was the benchmark once again for much of FP3 in Baku, at one point heading Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli by six tenths of a second.

But Verstappen gradually chipped away at his best time as the session moved towards its conclusion. Having been more than a second off with his first attempt on softs, he split the Mercedes on his next attempt, got within a tenth of Russell after that, and finally set the session's best time, a 1m43.922s, with a small slipstream assist from Charles Leclerc's Ferrari.

Verstappen had been on course to go faster still as the chequered flag fell, on what was his 11th lap on that set of soft tyres, but he locked up and took to the runoff at the tight Turn 15 left-hander for a second time in the session.

Nevertheless, Verstappen still topped an FP3 session for the first time this season, with Russell - who had a late lock-up of his own and just avoided skating into the barrier at the Turn 7 right-hander - 0.099s down in second.

Russell's Mercedes was one of three cars that Lewis Hamilton was able to gain a slipstream from along the main straight as he jumped to third at the end of the session. Hamilton had spent some time in the garage prior to that while Ferrari inspected his front-left brake.

Championship leader Antonelli ended up fourth, 0.351s down, with Leclerc six tenths back in fifth and Monza polesitter Pierre Gasly jumping up to sixth late on for Alpine.

The McLarens again were not in the picture. Oscar Piastri complained mid-session of having "very low confidence" into the first corner but he was the faster McLaren in seventh thanks to a tow, a tenth and a half ahead of team-mate Lando Norris.

Isack Hadjar was 1.2s off Red Bull team-mate Verstappen in ninth, without a tow assist and complaining of traffic, with Franco Colapinto making it two Alpines in the top 10 - just ahead of Williams's Carlos Sainz.

But the midfield pack looked particularly congested. Just half a second covered 10th down to 17th, with Cadillac's Sergio Perez again in that mix. He was 16th, 2.082s off the pace.

That meant Alex Albon (Williams) and both Racing Bulls drivers were in the bottom six, with Fernando Alonso a mildly encouraging 2.590s off the pace for Aston Martin in 20th.

Despite the wind picking up and a number of drivers missing apexes, Alonso's team-mate Lance Stroll had the only real incident of note when he clipped the pitwall through the first corner.

He initially thought that had caused a puncture but was then asked to stop the car and took to the runoff beyond the Turn 4 left-hander.
